meta.title: Swahili C1 Advanced
meta.subtitle: 1500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Swahili → English (see the Swahili, recall the meaning) and English → Swahili (see an English meaning, recall the Swahili). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1500 words for an advanced learner, aligned to C1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand a wide range of demanding, longer texts, and recognise implicit meaning' — a learner here is able to express ideas fluently and spontaneously without much obvious searching for expressions, to use language flexibly and effectively for social, academic and professional purposes, and to produce clear, well-structured, detailed text on complex subjects, showing controlled use of organisational patterns, connectors and cohesive devices. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Swahili that could be used here, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 99 of the 1500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — scholarship and language, belief, the political economy, history and the sea, the land and its life, the body and medicine, crafts and rites, and the words of reasoning — and the other 1401 are the commonest remaining words, counted by the WHOLE word (every form of a noun, every conjugated form of a verb added together) in two collections of real Swahili, written Swahili this time — CCMatrix, sentences mined from the web, and WikiMatrix, sentences from Swahili Wikipedia — because the subtitles and news site that ranked the lower levels are too small to rank words this rare, a word having to be common in both. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Verbs are shown as their infinitive (kusoma, to read) with their stem (-soma), which every tense is built on, and their negative infinitive; adjectives and possessives as their stem (-zuri, -angu) with the forms they take after three of the noun classes. The 1248 nouns show their class, which every adjective, verb and possessive agrees with, and their plural; there are 180 verbs. Real example sentences come with 195 of the 1500 words, three apiece for 16 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, noun classes and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: counted from CCMatrix and WikiMatrix (CC BY-SA, from Wikipedia), both as distributed by OPUS; only their counts are used, and no text from them is in the deck. Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
